quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Third conditional: 'had + past participle' pairs with 'would have + past participle' to imagine a different past.
quests.explanation: If-clause (If she had invested earlier) + result (she would have earned significantly more). Third conditional describes an unreal past situation and its imagined result — the opposite of what actually happened.
quests.textToSpeak: If she had invested earlier, she would have earned significantly more.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The negative result uses 'wouldn't have', a contraction of 'would not have'.
quests.explanation: If-clause (If the company had tested the software properly) + result (the crash wouldn't have happened). This shows a past mistake and the outcome that could have been prevented.
quests.textToSpeak: If the company had tested the software properly, the crash wouldn't have happened.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Never' slots between 'would' and 'have' for extra emphasis.
quests.explanation: If-clause (If the factory had followed regulations) + result (the spill would never have occurred). 'Would never have + past participle' strongly emphasizes that the event was entirely avoidable.
quests.textToSpeak: If the factory had followed regulations, the spill would never have occurred.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Sooner' is the comparative of 'soon', showing an earlier hypothetical timing.
quests.explanation: If-clause (If he had seen a doctor sooner) + result (the infection wouldn't have spread). This structure is common for reflecting on missed opportunities in the past.
quests.textToSpeak: If he had seen a doctor sooner, the infection wouldn't have spread.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Risen' is the past participle of 'rise' — remember, 'rise' has no direct object.
quests.explanation: If-clause (If the city had built more housing) + result (rents wouldn't have risen so sharply). 'Rise' is intransitive; things rise by themselves, unlike 'raise', which takes an object.
quests.textToSpeak: If the city had built more housing, rents wouldn't have risen so sharply.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The result clause states what they could have prevented.
quests.explanation: If-clause (If they had read the contract carefully) + result (they would have avoided the fee). Third conditional often expresses regret about a decision that led to an unwanted outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: If they had read the contract carefully, they would have avoided the fee.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: This is the inverted, more formal version of 'If the engineers had caught...'.
quests.explanation: Inverted if-clause (Had the engineers caught the flaw earlier) + result (the recall could have been avoided). Dropping 'if' and starting with 'Had' is a formal alternative used in writing and careful speech.
quests.textToSpeak: Had the engineers caught the flaw earlier, the recall could have been avoided.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Might have been' is a softer, less certain version of 'would have been'.
quests.explanation: Inverted if-clause (Had the government acted sooner) + result (the damage might have been far less severe). 'Might have' expresses a possible, not guaranteed, alternative outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: Had the government acted sooner, the damage might have been far less severe.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Start with 'Had'. No 'if' is needed in this inverted structure.
quests.explanation: Inverted if-clause (Had she followed the treatment plan closely) + result (recovery would have been quicker). This inversion is common in more formal spoken and written English.
quests.textToSpeak: Had she followed the treatment plan closely, recovery would have been quicker.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: After 'Not only', the subject and auxiliary verb switch places, just like in a question.
quests.explanation: Not only (emphatic opener) + did the stock rise (inverted clause) + but it also doubled within a year (second clause). Starting a sentence with 'Not only' requires question-style word order.
quests.textToSpeak: Not only did the stock rise, but it also doubled within a year.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Two connected achievements, joined by 'but... also'.
quests.explanation: Not only (emphatic opener) + did the new metro line reduce traffic (inverted clause) + but it also cut pollution (second clause). 'Not only... but also' links two positive results for extra emphasis.
quests.textToSpeak: Not only did the new metro line reduce traffic, but it also cut pollution.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Remember the inverted order right after 'Not only'.
quests.explanation: Not only (emphatic opener) + did the update fix the bug (inverted clause) + but it also improved battery life (second clause). This structure adds emphasis compared to simply joining two facts with 'and'.
quests.textToSpeak: Not only did the update fix the bug, but it also improved battery life.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'What...' introduces the cause; 'was' introduces the actual answer.
quests.explanation: Cleft sentence: What finally convinced him to quit smoking (the focus, as a noun clause) + was (linking verb) + his daughter's worried face (the answer). This structure puts special emphasis on the cause.
quests.textToSpeak: What finally convinced him to quit smoking was his daughter's worried face.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The second half answers the question raised by the first half.
quests.explanation: Cleft sentence: What surprised researchers most (the focus) + was (linking verb) + how quickly the ecosystem recovered (the answer). This pattern highlights the most surprising element of a situation.
quests.textToSpeak: What surprised researchers most was how quickly the ecosystem recovered.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The contrast 'not perfect timing' sharpens the main point.
quests.explanation: Cleft sentence: What matters most in investing (the focus) + is (linking verb) + patience, not perfect timing (the answer, with a contrast added). Adding 'not X' after the answer clarifies exactly what is meant.
quests.textToSpeak: What matters most in investing is patience, not perfect timing.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'It was...that...' wraps around the key time detail for emphasis.
quests.explanation: Cleft sentence: It was only after the outage (emphasized time) + that engineers found the real cause (rest of the sentence). This structure highlights exactly when something became true.
quests.textToSpeak: It was only after the outage that engineers found the real cause.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The emphasized part usually answers 'when did this really happen?'.
quests.explanation: Cleft sentence: It was only after the accident (emphasized time) + that the city added a traffic light (rest of the sentence). 'It was...that...' is especially useful for pointing out a delayed reaction.
quests.textToSpeak: It was only after the accident that the city added a traffic light.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Months of tests' is the emphasized time period before 'that'.
quests.explanation: Cleft sentence: It was only after months of tests (emphasized time) + that doctors identified the rare condition (rest of the sentence). This pattern often implies the answer took longer than expected.
quests.textToSpeak: It was only after months of tests that doctors identified the rare condition.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Had been approved' (passive + past perfect) happened before the noticing.
quests.explanation: Subject (The loan) + had been approved (past perfect passive) + before the bank noticed the error (later past event). Past perfect passive shows an action completed before another past action.
quests.textToSpeak: The loan had been approved before the bank noticed the error.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Two passive verbs in different tenses show the timeline clearly.
quests.explanation: Subject (The vulnerability) + had been reported (past perfect passive) + months before it was finally patched (later past passive event). This structure is useful for describing a gap between a warning and a fix.
quests.textToSpeak: The vulnerability had been reported months before it was finally patched.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The protection came first in time, so it uses past perfect.
quests.explanation: Subject (The wetlands) + had been protected (past perfect passive) + long before developers proposed the project (later past event). This word order makes the timeline of events completely unambiguous.
quests.textToSpeak: The wetlands had been protected long before developers proposed the project.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'The more..., the worse...' links two changes that grow together.
quests.explanation: Parallel comparison: The more the city grew (first change) + the worse the traffic became (linked second change). This 'the + comparative, the + comparative' pattern shows two things changing together.
quests.textToSpeak: The more the city grew, the worse the traffic became.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Both halves use 'the + comparative' and mirror each other in structure.
quests.explanation: Parallel comparison: The longer she waited (first change) + the harder the decision became (linked second change). Notice both clauses follow the identical 'the + comparative + subject + verb' pattern.
quests.textToSpeak: The longer she waited, the harder the decision became.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: This version drops the verbs entirely for a punchier, proverb-like feel.
quests.explanation: Parallel comparison: The riskier the investment (first change) + the greater the potential reward (linked second change). Verbs can often be omitted in this pattern when the meaning stays clear.
quests.textToSpeak: The riskier the investment, the greater the potential reward.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: Negative adverbs like 'rarely' at the start trigger question-style inversion.
quests.explanation: Rarely (negative frequency adverb) + does a single update change (inverted clause) + user habits so dramatically (rest of sentence). Starting with 'rarely' requires inverted word order, just like a question.
quests.textToSpeak: Rarely does a single update change user habits so dramatically.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Seldom' behaves exactly like 'rarely' — inversion follows.
quests.explanation: Seldom (negative frequency adverb) + do such small changes produce (inverted clause) + such lasting results (rest of sentence). 'Seldom' is a more formal synonym for 'rarely'.
quests.textToSpeak: Seldom do such small changes produce such lasting results.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Never' combines with past perfect for dramatic emphasis on an unprecedented event.
quests.explanation: Never (negative adverb) + had the market reacted (inverted past perfect) + so strongly to a single announcement (rest of sentence). This dramatic inversion is common in news and formal commentary.
quests.textToSpeak: Never had the market reacted so strongly to a single announcement.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Only after X' at the start also triggers inversion in the main clause.
quests.explanation: Only after the surgery (limiting time phrase) + did she realize (inverted clause) + how exhausted she truly was (rest of sentence). 'Only after/when/by' phrases trigger the same inversion as negative adverbs.
quests.textToSpeak: Only after the surgery did she realize how exhausted she truly was.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: The inverted clause follows the same pattern: auxiliary before subject.
quests.explanation: Only when construction finally ended (limiting time clause) + did the neighborhood feel calm again (inverted clause). This structure emphasizes just how long the wait for calm really was.
quests.textToSpeak: Only when construction finally ended did the neighborhood feel calm again.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and arrange the words in the correct order.
quests.hint: 'Only by + verb-ing' introduces the necessary method before the inverted clause.
quests.explanation: Only by testing extensively (limiting method phrase) + did the team catch the hidden flaw (inverted clause). This pattern stresses that thorough testing was the one thing that made the discovery possible.
quests.textToSpeak: Only by testing extensively did the team catch the hidden flaw.
